newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France reassures on EMU, but deficit question open.
newsitem.headline: France reassures on EMU, but deficit question open.

text.p: France and Germany offered fresh reassurance on Monday on European monetary union but left big questions unanswered on how they will solve their differences on the terms and conditions for a single currency.
Notably they disagree on how much budget deficits must be cut to qualify for monetary union in 1999, and on how far politicians can influence the exchange rate of the new euro.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told a news conference following a meeting of European Union finance ministers that France was determined to respect the Maastricht treaty and launch the new euro on time.
"We all must get ourselves into a position to be able to stick to the the January 1, 1999 date," he said.
But he declined to say how tough France's new Socialist-led government was ready to be on public finances.

While German Finance Minister Theo Waigel repeated on Monday that Germany planned to reduce its deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, Strauss-Kahn said he was "determined to respect what is said in the treaty".
The Maastricht treaty calls for countries to cut deficit/GDP ratios to, or towards three, leaving room for debate about how that should be interpreted.

Strauss-Kahn has already said France will not cut the deficit to 3.0 percent of GDP this year, though he said on Monday he was awaiting the results of an audit of public finances due on July 21 before making further comment.
Fears that France may ease up on deficit reduction have prompted calls from some in Germany for a delay to monetary union is Maastricht treaty criteria are not strictly respected.
That call was backed by Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm who said on Monday respect for the criteria must come first.

"My government has always been in favour of a strict interpretation of the criteria," he told Reuters Financial Television. "I hope we don't need a delay but you cannot start when everybody does not respect the criteria."

Strauss-Kahn, delving into another thorny area of Franco-German relations, also told his European partners that France wanted Article 109 of the Maastricht treaty implemented in full. Article 109 allows governments "to draw up general direction on exchange rate policy".

Germany is extremely sensitive to any political control of the exchange rate which might threaten the independence of the future European Central Bank, seen as its guarantor that the new euro will be as stable as the mark.
The issue is to be discussed during the next six months when Luxembourg holds the EU's rotating presidency.

Strauss-Kahn insisted however that Franco-German relations were as solid as ever and both were going in the same direction despite recent rows about a stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of the euro.
"There are sometimes stones on the road. What counts is the road," he said.
